title: The Wardrobe of Anderlecht
premise: Hazel Ashgrove, a piano tuner who reads houses through their radiators and pipes, inherits their grandmother's narrow Brussels townhouse in Anderlecht after decades of estrangement. Sorting the wardrobe, they find photographs of a woman named Margriet—a name no one in the family ever spoke—and a stranger at the funeral, Lucienne, claims to be her daughter. As Hazel tunes pianos across the city to pay for repairs, they uncover that Margriet was the grandmother's sister, erased after wartime collaboration, and that Lucienne holds letters proving Hazel's family took the house from hers. In the end, Hazel chooses co-ownership over quiet exile, renaming the house with both names and finally hearing themselves as part of its music.
about_author: Ivo Thornbury is the pen name of a former piano restorer who spent ten years tuning instruments in Brussels before turning to fiction. Their work explores how ordinary objects hold the weight of what families refuse to say aloud.

chapters.title: The Tuner's Ear
chapters.summary: Hazel arrives in Anderlecht for the funeral of a grandmother they barely knew, staying in the shuttered townhouse out of obligation rather than grief. At night they press a palm to the radiators and hear the house's long history humming. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: numb detachment masking an ache for belonging.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: At the funeral, a composed stranger named Lucienne approaches the family and calls them by an unfamiliar surname—Vermeulen—leaving Hazel's relatives cold and confused. Hazel alone follows her into the churchyard. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: first crack in the family's careful silence; curiosity displaces dread.

chapters.title: What the Wardrobe Keeps
chapters.summary: Sorting the grandmother's wardrobe, Hazel finds a false back panel holding photographs of two young women, one labeled 'Margriet, 1943,' and a key that fits nothing in the house. The radiator pipes seem to shift pitch when Hazel carries the photos room to room. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: haunted fascination; the house begins speaking.

chapters.title: Lucienne at the Door
chapters.summary: Lucienne appears on the doorstep claiming to be Margriet's daughter, asking not for money but for 'what was written down.' Hazel turns her away but cannot stop replaying her voice, which sounds uncannily like their own mother's. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: guilt and denial entwined; the past refuses eviction.

chapters.title: The Piano on Rue de Fiennes
chapters.summary: To fund roof repairs, Hazel takes tuning work across Brussels, including a battered upright in a café where an old patron remembers the Vermeulen sisters—one who played, one who signed papers for the occupiers. POV: Hazel, with the patron's recounted memory. Emotional beat: the comfortable family story starts to rot from within.

chapters.title: Letters Behind the Plaster
chapters.summary: Following the radiator hum to a cold bedroom, Hazel pries loose a pipe collar and finds a tin of unsent letters: the grandmother writing to Margriet for forty years, begging forgiveness she never mailed. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: devastating intimacy with a stranger-grandmother; grief finally arrives.

chapters.title: The Family Convenes
chapters.summary: Hazel's mother and uncle arrive to sell the house quickly, dismissing the letters as sentiment and Lucienne as a fraud. When Hazel mentions Margriet, the uncle's fury reveals he has always known more than he admitted. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: rising conflict; loyalty to family curdles into complicity.

chapters.title: Margriet's Side
chapters.summary: Hazel visits Lucienne's cramped flat in Schaerbeek and hears the other history: Margriet's collaboration was coerced, her punishment was erasure, and the house legally should have passed to her line. Lucienne offers the deeds—not as threat, but as proof she never wanted a fight, only acknowledgment. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: empathy overturns inherited judgment.

chapters.title: The Auction Notice
chapters.summary: The uncle lists the house while Hazel sleeps; movers arrive at dawn. In the climax, Hazel plays the grandmother's unplayed piano—out of tune, defiantly loud—while reading one letter aloud to the assembled family, forcing them to hear the name Margriet spoken in the house itself. Lucienne stands witness at the door. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: rupture and courage; silence broken beyond repair.

chapters.title: Two Names on the Bell
chapters.summary: Weeks later, the sale is halted and redrawn as shared ownership between Hazel and Lucienne; the uncle walks away, but Hazel's mother stays for tea, tentative and changed. Hazel retunes every piano in the house and engraves both surnames beside the doorbell. POV: Hazel. Emotional beat: resolution—belonging chosen, not inherited; identity rebuilt from honest inheritance.
